title: Kelty flays ALP bid for cash reforms
full_text:
ALP NATIONAL CONFERENCE Former union heavyweight and Labor veteran Bill Kelty has eviscerated the Albanese government over its plan to hand sweeping regulatory powers to Australia’s competition watchdog and the Reserve Bank to safeguard the future of cash.
Labor this month introduced legislation it claims will secure a sustainable future for the distribution of cash after a series of industry-negotiated bailouts for Australia’s only cash distributor, Linfox Armaguard, and stalled talks over an independent pricing model.
Mr Kelty, in his capacity as a non-executive director of Linfox Armaguard, delivered a blistering testimony to the Senate economics legislation committee, saying the bill in its current form was a “policy of lunacy and stupidity” and a $400m crisis funding pool was a “terrible” use of taxpayer money.
“Frankly this country can do better than that. We can do better than that, this country deserves better than that,” Mr Kelty said.
“We actually think, to be frank about it, that when people get paid so little in unemployment benefits, when hospitals are under pressure, where we have an inadequacy in terms of nursing, when teachers are underpaid in this country, that there are better things for society to allocate (money to).” Crisis resolution provisions included in the legislation hand emergency powers to the RBA to place cash distributors under statutory management or compulsorily transfer all or part of the “shares or business” of a cash distribution company.
Peter Fox, executive chair of Linfox Armaguard and eldest son of business magnate Lindsay Fox, said the provisions amounted to nationalisation of the cash distribution sector “by stealth”.
“The proposed legislation you are here contemplating is blatantly unfair,” Mr Fox said.
“In the face of what we have achieved to date without any help from the government, this is a nationalisation by stealth.
“It is not in our common or collective interests to be doing so.” Armaguard has spent the past few years with a cloud over its financial viability, after a price war forced it to merge with competitor Prosegur in 2023 – greenlit by the Australian Competition & Consumer Commission subject to undertakings set to expire in September.
Since then the country’s major banks along with Coles, Woolworths, Australia Post and Wesfarmers have supplied the beleaguered cash distributor with more than $100m in financial support.
Mr Fox used the hearing to say the passage of the government’s legislation could derail work towards an independent pricing mechanism, agreed to by the Australian Banking Association but yet to be submitted by Armaguard to the ACCC for consideration.
The Linfox Armaguard board is set to consider the pricing model as designed at a meeting next week, but has been urged by the ABA to submit it as soon as possible.
The legislation also hands the ACCC powers to regulate Armaguard’s services and prices in regional areas, a move watchdog chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb said was in the public interest. Representatives from Treasury and the RBA said the expanded regulatory powers and crisis resolution framework were standard for “entities that have a significant and critical role in the financial system”.
